summary: 8月19日上午，中国航天事业跨越了一个重大门槛。中国航天公司蓝箭航天在中国西北部发射一枚火箭后不久，其助推器（将火箭推入轨道所需的部件）成功分离并返回地球。这是中国公司首次在陆地上回收火箭，六周前，中国首屈一指的国有航天承包商在南海进行了首次火箭回收。这些事件标志着中国可重复使用火箭发射的曙光——这种能力将释放巨大的潜力。
content:
8月19日上午，中国航天事业跨越了一个重大门槛。中国航天公司蓝箭航天在中国西北部发射一枚火箭后不久，其助推器（将火箭推入轨道所需的部件）成功分离并返回地球。这是中国公司首次在陆地上回收火箭，六周前，中国首屈一指的国有航天承包商在南海进行了首次火箭回收。这些事件标志着中国可重复使用火箭发射的曙光，这种能力将释放中国蓬勃发展的航天工业的巨大潜力。

华盛顿对这些事态发展的反应一直很冷淡。 [美国](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/regions/united-states) 的发射次数和在轨卫星数量仍然是其他任何国家的两倍多。但中国正在迎头赶上。 2020年至2025年间，中国企业每年发射的火箭数量增加了一倍多，从39枚增加到92枚。中国实体已申请了数十万颗通信卫星的许可证，中国航天公司也在激增。其中许多，例如蓝箭空间，相对较新，但已经具有创新性。
这一进展具有经济和军事意义。中国公司可能很快就会与美国公司展开竞争，为全球大片地区提供卫星互联网等天基服务。与此同时，中国人民解放军将太空优势视为赢得未来战争的关键，正在开发一系列太空能力以及一套可以攻击卫星的武器。这对依赖太空进行通信、态势感知和导航以及进行精确打击和接收导弹警告的美军构成了严重风险。

中国作为太空强国的发展应该给美国敲响警钟。 [冷战](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/tags/cold-war)结束后，华盛顿开始认为其在太空的主导地位是理所当然的。它再也无力这样做了。随着北京航天工业的进步，其成本优势将使美国公司的竞争变得更加困难，而中国的军事能力将增加太空成为未来冲突战场的风险。美国无懈可击的太空力量时代即将结束，华盛顿别无选择，只能适应。

### 爆炸！
中国的太空计划可以追溯到 20 世纪 50 年代，当时中国领导人毛泽东发起了中国人民解放军现代化和推动技术创新的努力。 1970年，[中国](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/regions/china)发射了第一颗卫星，并在20世纪80年代将空间技术研究列为国家重点。但中国太空计划的分水岭发生在 1990-91 年海湾战争期间，当时美军对天基资产的熟练运用使得规模相对较小但技术先进的联盟在短短几天内击败了伊拉克军队。卫星使美军能够在困难的沙漠地形中航行，为指挥官提供更快、更准确的战场信息，并使士兵能够在长距离内无缝协调。北京尚未意识到自己落后了多少，立即采取行动追赶。

在接下来的几年里，解放军的条令强调先进技术（尤其是卫星）对于战争的重要性日益增加。我

【原文 English Original】
On the morning of August 19, China’s space industry crossed a major threshold. Shortly after the Chinese aerospace company LandSpace launched a rocket in northwestern China, its booster—the part needed to thrust the rocket into orbit—successfully detached and landed back on earth. It was the first time a Chinese firm recovered a rocket on land, and it came six weeks after the country’s first-ever rocket recovery, carried out in the South China Sea by China’s premier state-owned space contractor. These events mark the dawn of China’s reusable rocket launch—a capability that will unlock enormous potential in the country’s booming space industry.

Washington’s response to these developments has been muted. The [United States](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/regions/united-states) still conducts more than twice as many launches and has more satellites in orbit than any other country. But China is catching up. Between 2020 and 2025, the number of rockets launched annually by Chinese companies more than doubled, from 39 to 92. Chinese entities have applied for licenses for hundreds of thousands of communications satellites, and Chinese space companies are proliferating. Many of them, such as LandSpace, are relatively new but already innovative.

This progress has both economic and military implications. Chinese companies could soon compete with U.S. firms to provide vast swaths of the globe with space-based services such as satellite Internet. Meanwhile, the People’s Liberation Army (PLA), which sees space superiority as essential to winning future wars, is developing a range of space capabilities as well as a suite of weapons that can attack satellites. This poses a serious risk to the U.S. military, which depends on space for communications, situational awareness, and navigation, as well as for conducting precision strikes and receiving missile warnings.

China’s development as a space power should be a wake-up call for the United States. After the end of the [Cold War](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/tags/cold-war), Washington began to take its dominance in space for granted. It can no longer afford to do so. As Beijing’s space industry advances, its cost advantages will make it much harder for U.S. companies to compete, and China’s military capabilities will increase the risk that space becomes a battlefield in future conflicts. The era of unassailable U.S. space power is ending, and Washington has no choice but to adapt.

### BLASTOFF!

China’s space program dates to the 1950s, when Chinese leader Mao Zedong initiated efforts to modernize the PLA and boost technological innovation. In 1970, [China](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/regions/china) launched its first satellite, and in the 1980s, it made space technology research a national priority. But the watershed moment for China’s space program occurred during the 1990–91 Gulf War, when the U.S. military’s adept use of space-based assets allowed a relatively small but technologically advanced coalition to defeat Iraq’s army in just a few days. Satellites allowed U.S. forces to navigate difficult desert terrain, gave commanders information about the battlefield with greater speed and accuracy, and enabled soldiers to coordinate seamlessly across long distances. Beijing, which had not realized just how far behind it was, leaped into action to catch up.

In the years that followed, PLA doctrine emphasized the growing importance of advanced technology, especially satellites, for warfighting. In 2000, the Chinese military began developing its own satellite-powered navigation service, called BeiDou, so that it would not have to rely on U.S.-operated GPS. In 2015, the PLA created the Strategic Support Force, a now defunct organization that consolidated China’s space, cyber, and electronic warfare missions, with the aim of accelerating the country’s space progress. That same year, a Chinese government white paper identified outer space as a critical national security domain. China has since created spacecraft for communications; navigation; and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance that would have been unimaginable to PLA officials who observed Desert Storm.

Encouraging commercial space activity has become one of China’s main tools for expanding its space program. In 2014, Beijing opened parts of the space sector to private investment, and more than 400 Chinese commercial space companies have since sprouted. Beijing and provincial governments have provided commercial space firms with financing through state-backed investment funds, subsidized factory upgrades and rocket launches, and given private companies access to government test facilities and technologies. In 2025, commercial space missions accounted for 54 percent of China’s national total, and commercial satellites made up 84 percent of Chinese spacecraft placed in orbit. China’s broad space-industrial ecosystem, composed of commercial companies, state-owned enterprises, research institutes, and universities, has allowed the country to eliminate its dependence on GPS and paved the way for the development of new domestic remote sensing and satellite communications companies.

In reusable rocket technology, the U.S. company SpaceX has enjoyed an enormous advantage, conducting five out of every six launches in the United States. But China’s two controlled recoveries of rocket boosters in July and August suggest that it could be a real competitor to the United States within a decade. Reusable rockets drive down the cost and increase the speed of space launches significantly; should China master the technology, it could develop large satellite constellations much more easily.

Reusable launches will also allow China to develop space-based Internet capabilities to compete with SpaceX’s dominant Starlink network, an extensive satellite Internet system with connectivity that rivals many land-based networks and which has been crucial for Ukraine in its defense against Russia. Although Chinese companies are still in the early stages of developing this technology, they are scaling fast. The entities operating the Guowang and Qianfan satellite constellations, which intend to compete with Starlink, plan to launch nearly 30,000 communications satellites over the next decade or so. These systems are currently much smaller than Starlink, which has more than 11,000 satellites in orbit, but they could eventually become legitimate alternatives. Qianfan already has trial agreements with Brazil, Kazakhstan, Malaysia, and Turkey for the use of its satellite network.

### ROCKET SCIENCE

China’s commercial space development has gone hand in hand with a growing ability to use space to support its military modernization. Beijing has spent decades studying the U.S. military’s use of satellites, and it is now developing its own national security–related space capabilities. According to the Pentagon, China operates more than 500 satellites that can conduct intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance missions, in addition to its satellite-enabled positioning system, allowing the PLA to locate and track U.S. and allied forces around the world. PLA strategists have identified Defense Department space assets as valuable targets because the U.S. military depends on them for nearly every step of what it calls the “kill chain”: finding, aiming at, and striking targets, and then assessing the results.

To exploit U.S. dependence on satellites, Beijing is investing in antisatellite weapons. Since 2007, when it conducted its first successful test of an antisatellite missile, China has developed other tools, including electronic warfare and directed-energy weapons, which can interfere with satellite signals or damage sensors without physically destroying satellites. Chinese spacecraft can also execute increasingly sophisticated maneuvers: in 2022, a Chinese satellite called Shijian-21 attached itself to a defunct Chinese satellite and moved it into a different orbit. Such an action could be benign—it could be used to repair and refuel satellites or remove debris—but it could also enable Chinese platforms to manipulate other spacecraft, including U.S. military satellites. Beijing’s ability to take down U.S. satellites could pose an especially serious challenge for the U.S. military in East Asia, where, in the case of conflict, China would be much less dependent on space-based assets than the United States.

China’s space rise is already influencing broader international security dynamics. During Russia’s full-scale invasion of [Ukraine](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/regions/ukraine), in 2022, Chinese firms provided satellite imagery of the battlefield that helped Russian forces conduct military operations. Throughout the war in Iran, Chinese entities have also supplied Tehran with satellite imagery, including images of a base in Jordan that Iran struck in July, resulting in the deaths of three American service members. As China’s commercial space sector expands, so could these relationships, giving more countries and nonstate actors without advanced space programs access to their benefits. Such expanded access could be used during natural disasters or other emergencies to save lives. But it could also provide adversaries with the ability to more effectively target U.S. and allied forces across the globe.

### MISSION CRITICAL

As China’s space power grows, Washington has moved to protect some of its satellite networks. The U.S. Space Force has diversified the placement of some of its most sensitive assets and increased procurement of new satellites. Such investments are useful but insufficient to address the United States’ vulnerabilities. Given the capabilities that China already has or will develop soon, there are now many possible scenarios in which the U.S. military would have to operate when satellite communications are denied or degraded, GPS signals are jammed, and intelligence from orbit is restricted.

The U.S. military should invest in nascent technologies, such as inertial navigation systems and quantum sensors, which could one day help its forces move with precision without GPS. It should also invest in emerging alternatives to satellites, such as high-altitude relays, which include drones or balloons that operate closer to Earth and can link communications networks; laser-enabled communications, which use light to transmit information and are difficult to disrupt; and mesh networks, which automatically reroute signals around nodes that have been destroyed, making communications more resilient. Mechanisms for delegating decision-making will be even more essential than in the past, as the danger of disconnection increases.

Washington should also increase its efforts to foster a more competitive domestic launch industry. The United States leads the world in space launches largely because of SpaceX. Although the company is an enormous asset, its near monopoly is a risk. If technical failures or damage to launch infrastructure were to interrupt SpaceX’s operations, the United States’ ability to launch satellites would be severely curtailed. This year, SpaceX announced plans to retire the Falcon 9, its main reusable rocket. The Falcon 9 will eventually be replaced by Starship, a new high-capacity rocket that will carry more satellites into orbit with each launch. But the beginning of the phase-out has already created a launch shortage that threatens the continued development of the U.S. space economy. To mitigate this risk, Washington should continue awarding government contracts to more companies.

> SpaceX is an enormous asset to the United States, but its near monopoly is a risk.

In addition to investing in launch capacity, the United States should provide support to companies building emerging space technologies that have important national security applications but which struggle to attract sufficient commercial demand in their early years—an approach it took with SpaceX starting in th

title: Taiwan coastguard wards off 16 mainland ships as Beijing turns up the pressure
zh_title: 北京加大施压 台湾海警拦截16艘大陆船只
summary: 台湾海岸警卫队表示，一天之内，16艘中国大陆船只驶入台湾自行定义的限制水域，并通过协调一致的多管齐下行动将其拦截，专家表示，这表明北京海上压力策略的转变。据海巡署称，这些船只包括 12 艘海岸警卫队和科考船，以及四艘渔船，周日在花莲以东、屏东以南、高雄西南部以及台湾控制的东沙群岛周围海域同时作业。 “CGA自始至终监控海事局势
content:
台湾海岸警卫队表示，一天之内，16艘中国大陆船只驶入台湾自行定义的限制水域，并通过协调一致的多管齐下行动将其拦截，专家表示，这表明北京海上压力策略的转变。

据海巡署称，这些船只包括 12 艘海岸警卫队和科考船，以及四艘渔船，周日在花莲以东、屏东以南、高雄西南部以及台湾控制的东沙群岛周围海域同时作业。

中国海警在周日的一份声明中表示，“中国海警在整个行动过程中监视了海上局势，并立即派遣海警船只前往前沿阵地，对大陆船只进行严密监视，并发布警告命令其离开。”

该机构将这些活动描述为“[混合战争](https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military/article/3220645/chinese-general-calls-military-prepare-hybrid-modern-warfare?module=inline&pgtype=article)”，旨在扩大北京的管辖权主张。

它指责北京“名义上执法，实际上扩大权力”，以营造其对该海域行使管辖权的印象。

此次行动正值安全专家越来越担心北京越来越多地利用海岸警卫队、海上执法船和科考船在台湾周边施加压力，而不是主要依靠中国人民解放军。
02:55

台湾结束年度军演，包括为解放军海上封锁做准备

桃园国防大学解放军事务教授马振坤表示，北京今年的重点已逐渐从海军主导的灰色地带行动转向通过海岸警卫队、海上巡逻和研究船维护管辖权。

马云说：“对于北京来说，此类措施比传统的军事灰色地带行动能产生更具体的成果。”

他将这一做法描述为“离岛夺周边海域”的战略——逐步挤压台湾及其离岛周边海域，但又不引发彻底的军事冲突。

马英九表示，这种做法在南海已经很明显，而且在台湾以东的海域以及金门、马祖、东沙和台湾控制的南沙群岛太平岛周围的海域也越来越多地出现。金门又名金门。

他的评估大体呼应了国际战略研究所 10 月 8 日的分析，该研究所称，自 6 月以来，北京加强了台湾东部的执法、海上监视、渔业和研究活动。

这家总部位于伦敦的智库将中国大陆行为体的扩散描述为北京灰色地带战略的重大发展，可能旨在在台湾周围建立一个涉及军事和民事机构的更复杂的海洋治理体系。
活动的增加也引发了人们的疑问：台湾是否能够在不造成自身海岸警卫队资源紧张的情况下可持续地对船只做出反应。

美国退役海军四星上将、美国太平洋司令部前司令丹尼斯·布莱尔上周在台北举行的海上安全会议上发表视频讲话时表示，台湾不应自动跟踪每艘大陆船只或飞机。

相反，台北应该根据威胁程度分配有限的资源，保留运营能力

【原文 English Original】
Taiwan’s coastguard said it warded off 16 mainland Chinese vessels in one day after they sailed into the island’s self-defined restricted waters in a coordinated, multi-pronged operation that experts say points to a shift in Beijing’s maritime pressure tactics.

The vessels – 12 coastguard and research ships, as well as four fishing boats – operated simultaneously on Sunday in waters east of Hualien, south of Pingtung, southwest of Kaohsiung and around the Taiwan-controlled Dongsha Islands, according to the Coast Guard Administration (CGA).

“The CGA monitored the maritime situation throughout the operation and immediately dispatched coastguard vessels to forward positions, where they closely monitored the mainland vessels and broadcast warnings ordering them to leave,” it said in a statement on Sunday.

The agency described the activities as “[hybrid warfare](https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military/article/3220645/chinese-general-calls-military-prepare-hybrid-modern-warfare?module=inline&pgtype=article)” intended to expand Beijing’s jurisdictional claims.

It accused Beijing of pursuing “law enforcement in name, expansion of authority in reality” to create the impression that it exercised jurisdiction over the waters.

The operation comes amid growing concern among security experts that Beijing is increasingly using coastguard, maritime law enforcement and research vessels to apply pressure around Taiwan, rather than relying predominantly on the People’s Liberation Army.

02:55

Taiwan concludes annual war games, including preparing for PLA sea blockade

Ma Chen-kun, a professor of PLA affairs at National Defence University in Taoyuan, said Beijing’s focus had gradually shifted this year from navy-led grey-zone operations towards asserting jurisdiction through coastguard, maritime patrol and research vessels.

“For Beijing, such measures produce more concrete results than conventional military grey-zone operations,” Ma said.

He described the approach as a strategy of “leaving the islands but taking away the surrounding seas” – gradually squeezing the waters around Taiwan and its outlying islands without provoking an outright military conflict.

Ma said the approach, already evident in the South China Sea, was increasingly being seen in waters east of Taiwan as well as around Quemoy, Matsu, Dongsha and the Taiwan-controlled Taiping Island in the South China Sea’s Spratly archipelago. Quemoy is also known as Kinmen.

His assessment broadly echoes an October 8 analysis by the International Institute for Strategic Studies, which said Beijing had stepped up law enforcement, maritime surveillance, fisheries and research activities east of Taiwan since June.

The London-based think tank described the proliferation of mainland Chinese actors as a significant development in Beijing’s grey-zone strategy, potentially aimed at establishing a more complex system of maritime governance around Taiwan involving military and civilian agencies.

The increased activity has also raised questions over whether Taiwan can sustainably respond vessel-for-vessel without straining its own coastguard resources.

Dennis Blair, a retired US Navy four-star admiral and former commander of the US Pacific Command, said in a video address to a maritime security conference in Taipei last week that Taiwan should not automatically shadow every mainland ship or aircraft.

Taipei should instead allocate its limited resources according to the level of threat, retain operational flexibility and strengthen maritime surveillance, law enforcement and self-defence capabilities, he said.

02:04

Philippines accuses China of firing a water cannon at its vessels for a second day

Taipei has increasingly looked to learn from the Philippines and its policy of “active transparency”, under which Manila has publicised confrontations with mainland Chinese vessels in the South China Sea.

Taiwan’s coastguard plans to send a vessel carrying about 100 officers and students to the Philippines next October, its first such visit in 53 years. Taipei also [donated](https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military/article/3368788/why-taiwans-coastguard-vessel-transfer-philippines-has-sparked-double-outcry?module=inline&pgtype=article) a retired patrol vessel to Manila last month.

Taiwan’s National Security Council deputy secretary general Lii Wen has called for greater technological and maritime law enforcement cooperation between the two in areas including maritime domain awareness, unmanned systems and less-lethal weapons.

Sunday’s operation was the latest in a series of encounters this month. Taiwan’s coastguard said it had driven mainland coastguard vessels away from waters around Dongsha on 11 occasions this year, involving 14 vessel appearances before the latest operation.

Since the start of this month, it has warded off 29 mainland coastguard, research, survey and fishing vessel appearances, including 16 from Sunday.

In a more serious incident on October 1, a Taiwanese coastguard vessel [used a water cannon](https://www.scmp.com/news/china/politics/article/3369634/taiwan-coastguard-uses-water-cannons-warn-mainland-chinese-fishing-vessel?module=inline&pgtype=article) to drive away a mainland fishing boat that refused to leave restricted waters near the Dongsha Islands, prompting a strong protest from Beijing.

09:58

Will Batanes become the next South China Sea flashpoint?

For Ma, the broader significance lies in Beijing’s apparent effort to turn repeated peacetime activity into assertions of jurisdiction – pressure that remains below the threshold of armed conflict but could gradually reshape practices in waters surrounding Taiwan.

Blair warned that the threshold would change sharply if Beijing escalated pressure by intercepting or boarding commercial vessels, forcing them to change course or imposing an effective blockade.

Such actions, he said, would move beyond grey-zone coercion and amount to acts of war.

Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

title: Moving Manufacturing From China To Mexico
summary: ### Moving Manufacturing From China to Mexico: The Complete Guide When China's COVID-zero lockdowns and its aggression toward Taiwan started spooking foreign companies in 2022, the [international manufacturing lawyers](https://harris-sliwos
content:
### Moving Manufacturing From China to Mexico: The Complete Guide

When China's COVID-zero lockdowns and its aggression toward Taiwan started spooking foreign companies in 2022, the [international manufacturing lawyers](https://harris-sliwoski.com/practice-areas/international-manufacturing-law/) at my firm began getting a steady stream of calls and emails from companies looking to leave China. Most wanted to know about Mexico, and some of the companies calling us were themselves Chinese or Taiwanese. The tariff wars since then have given companies more reasons to look south. Mexico makes sense for many of them. But companies that go into Mexico expecting to find China with a shorter shipping route are in for an expensive education.

Starting in 2022, my good friend Andrew Hupert and I wrote a long series of posts for this blog on what leaving China for Mexico actually involves. Nobody was better suited to write about this than Andrew. I first met him in Shanghai in 2003, and over the following two decades I came to rely deeply on his practical business wisdom, especially about China. When my firm stepped up its China practice, he was one of my go-to people on all things China. He was a business school professor who taught negotiation around the world, and he spent more than 20 years in Asia, living and working in Shanghai, Taipei, Hong Kong, and Saigon. Though he had tied his career to China, he, like me, was an early believer in a post-China manufacturing world. He moved to Thailand and then Vietnam, and when Mexico began emerging as a leading replacement for China manufacturing, he moved to Monterrey and then Oaxaca, and became fluent in Spanish. He spent his last years there helping companies, especially companies leaving China, set up and run operations in Mexico. Few people had spent as much time thinking about how the two countries compared, and fewer still had Andrew's willingness to say exactly what he thought.

Andrew died of a heart attack in Oaxaca in October 2024, at 61. I wrote about him and our friendship in [Remembering Andrew Hupert](https://harris-sliwoski.com/chinalawblog/remembering-andrew-hupert-international-business-guru/). This guide brings our Mexico work together in one place and updates it for 2026. Most of the business and cultural observations are Andrew's, drawn from his years running and advising operations in both countries. The legal and trade analysis is mine, informed by my firm's [affiliated lawyers in Mexico City](https://harris-sliwoski.com/location/mexico-city/) and the United States, and by many of the conclusions Andrew and I reached together over the years. Andrew is no longer here to update his words, so I have done that as best I can. Where events have proved us right or wrong, I say so. When I quote him, the words are his as he wrote them. I want readers to understand where his observations came from and why I continue to think they matter.

### Why Companies Are Leaving China

In early 2023, Andrew and I wrote that running a supply chain entirely through China had become a bet against the house, the kind that ends with the gambler up a ton at midnight and borrowing bus fare home by morning. The trade numbers seemed to argue otherwise. U.S.-China trade had hit a record $690 billion in 2022, and plenty of companies took that as vindication of their decision to stay. Multinationals were reading the situation differently. Their supply chain planners, the Lean Production and Six Sigma people who treat unnecessary risk as a sin, were piling into Mexico, as Unilever's $400 million commitment to a new plant in Nuevo León showed that same month. When a Chinese surveillance balloon was shot down over the United States that February, we predicted that cooler heads would not prevail. Washington, we said, would keep changing the economics of China supply chains by every means available, and Beijing would answer each new U.S. restriction with its own. We saw little reason to expect either government to put the interests of companies caught in the middle ahead of its own political priorities.

We put governments at the top of the list of likely supply chain shocks and said the damage would most likely come through mistakes, meaning bad regulations written and enforced for non-economic goals. Would governments knowingly hurt their own economies for a good soundbite? "Yes. Of course they would. We expected U.S. customs to demand ever more detailed proof that your goods were not made with forced labor in Xinjiang. Complying would trap your China staff in a catch-22, because trying to trace the origin of your materials could get them "invited to tea" by the authorities. We also expected Beijing to retaliate, since, as we put it, "Beijing will not apologize; it will reply." China has a long record of using trade to punish countries that anger it, including Japan, Norway, Canada, South Korea, Australia, and Lithuania. And we warned that after the disruptions of 2021 and 2022, no owner or fiduciary could credibly claim a China supply chain disruption was impossible to foresee. Many of our clients already had China exit and evacuation plans, and we told readers they should too. That advice was based on what we were already seeing companies struggle with, long before the current tariff battles. See [Doing Business with China and Your Reputation Risks](https://harris-sliwoski.com/chinalawblog/doing-business-with-china-and-your-reputation-risks/) and [Repeat After Me: Trade Relations Between the United States and China Will Only Get Worse](https://harris-sliwoski.com/chinalawblog/repeat-after-me-trade-relations-between-the-united-states-and-china-will-only-get-worse/).

Tariffs and trade restrictions have since vindicated much of what we wrote. In 2023, Mexico overtook China as the top source of U.S. goods imports, at $475.6 billion to China's $427.2 billion, with China's total down 20 percent from 2022. Real U.S. imports from China fell 28 percent in 2025 alone, and by year-end the average U.S. tariff on Chinese goods was near 50 percent, up from 21 percent when the second Trump administration took office. Beijing retaliated most effectively with rare earth export controls. It suspended its expanded October 2025 controls for one year, until November 10, 2026, but its April 2025 controls on seven medium and heavy rare earths remain in force. The forced-labor scrutiny we predicted has also become a basis for tariffs. In July 2026, the U.S. Trade Representative imposed tariffs on goods from 60 economies, China and Mexico among them, after finding that they had failed to impose and effectively enforce bans on imports made with forced labor. Our biggest mistake was assuming North American trade would remain politically protected. We underestimated just how willing Washington would be to make life difficult for companies manufacturing in Mexico, a subject I discuss below.

Companies that left China early told us their decisions had paid off. In that same 2023 series, Andrew and I passed along what clients who had moved their manufacturing elsewhere were saying. One said he slept better, both because he worried less about his supply chain and because he felt better about no longer supporting such a brutal regime. Another had left before COVID, which let it avoid the China tariffs, underprice its competitors, and take a good chunk of market share while those competitors scrambled to catch up. Others said they were hiring people who chose them because they had nothing to do with China. Still others had customers choosing them because their products did not come from China, whether to reduce supply chain risk or reputational risk. These were business owners explaining what had happened to their companies, and their experiences were far more persuasive than another consultant's presentation about geopolitical risk. We also said the most unforgivable sin foreign companies committed in China was going there without an exit strategy. I still believe that, and I would build an exit strategy into any Mexico plan from the start as well.

**Which Manufacturing Risks Can You Actually Control?**

One of the most important differences between manufacturing in China and Mexico is how much control you have over the risks your business faces. Every country has problems. Factories lose power, employees leave, suppliers fail, and shipments get delayed. You can reduce many of these risks by investigating your suppliers, choosing your location carefully, and making sure you have alternative sources of supply. You can never eliminate every manufacturing risk, but there is a great deal you can do to keep ordinary business problems from becoming disasters.

Many of Mexico's biggest manufacturing risks fall into that category. Security is a serious concern, but you can investigate specific locations and arrange safer transportation. Labor laws are demanding, but you can hire Mexican employment lawyers and structure your operation to comply with them. Infrastructure varies considerably, but you can check whether a proposed site has reliable power and water before committing to it. None of these precautions guarantees that your operation will run smoothly. They do, however, give you meaningful ways to reduce your exposure.

China presents some risks that no amount of good management can bring under your control. You can investigate your suppliers and trace your materials, but you cannot eliminate the possibility that U.S. Customs will detain your goods over forced-labor concerns. You cannot prevent Beijing from imposing export restrictions or Washington from raising tariffs. You can prepare for a crisis involving Taiwan, but you cannot prevent one. A company can do everything right inside its Chinese factory and still find its business badly damaged by a political decision made thousands of miles away. That is what makes these risks especially troubling. The company has very little ability to influence the decisions that create them.

Mexico has political risks of its own, as the 2026 USMCA review and the latest tariffs demonstrate. A Mexican manufacturer cannot control what Washington decides about North American trade any more than a Chinese manufacturer can control U.S. policy toward China. I would never suggest otherwise. But when comparing countries, I would pay particular attention to which risks you can realistically manage and which ones can overwhelm your business regardless of how carefully you operate. That distinction is one of the strongest reasons many companies have decided they would rather manufacture in Mexico.

**Who Can Still Stay in China**

Andrew's test turned on what you make and who buys it. Several kinds of companies can probably stay in China: those that provide services to Chinese B2B markets, produce for sale in China and Asia, or specialize in multinational supply chains. Companies that depend on an end-to-end global presence, such as hotels, travel companies, and financial services firms, can also stay, as can those big enough to run separate supply chains for separate markets. Companies that need materials, components, technology, or processes available only in China are a maybe. Their position keeps deteriorating, and nobody should want to be the last international manufacturer in China. A company running a low-cost strategy built on small runs of pre-sold products, less-than-container-load shipping, probably cannot stay. The important question is whether your own business falls into one of the categories that still makes economic sense there.

### Is Mexico Right for Your Company?

Andrew's starting point, from the first post of our series, was that comparing China and Mexico is not comparing apples to apples. The same product may leave the factory gate in both countries, but setting up and running operations in them involves very different systems. China's economy is highly structured and centrally planned. Mexico's is decentralized and reactive, an

title: Vivian Kong urges elite sports upgrade to boost Hong Kong's soft power
zh_title: 江若珩促精英体育升级提升香港软实力
summary: 香港立法会议员、前奥运击剑运动员江文慧呼吁优化精英体育训练体系，称运动员是香港软实力的最佳广告。在立法会辩论之前，她概述了四个目标，包括人才管道、体育科学、大湾区合作和国际合作 [![图片 1: Adam](https://clb.org.hk/en/static/img/editors/clb-adam-192.png)](https://clb.org.hk/en/desks/clb-desk) 作者：[Adam](https://clb.org.hk/en/desks/clb-desk)，主编2026 年 10 月 19 日，香港时间 17:35 · 阅读 2 分钟 优化精英运动训练体系，提升香港运动能力
content:
香港
立法会议员、前奥运击剑运动员江文慧呼吁优化精英体育训练体系，称运动员是香港软实力的最佳广告。在立法会辩论之前，她概述了四个目标，包括人才管道、体育科学、大湾区合作和国际合作。

[![图片1：Adam](https://clb.org.hk/en/static/img/editors/clb-adam-192.png)](https://clb.org.hk/en/desks/clb-desk)

作者：[Adam](https://clb.org.hk/en/desks/clb-desk)，主编

香港时间 2026 年 10 月 19 日 17:35 · 阅读时间 2 分钟

运动员出身的立法会议员江文慧表示，优化的精英体育训练体系将增强香港运动员的竞争优势，并成为香港在全球舞台上最强大的软实力展示。

继香港在第 20 届亚运会历史性地夺得 54 枚奖牌之后，她在周三立法会就一项改善精英体育训练和支持系统的动议进行辩论之前发表了上述言论。这位前奥运会击剑金牌得主在接受《旗帜报》姊妹刊物《星岛日报》的采访时，表达了对运动员发展和机构支持持续进步的强烈支持。

“运动员为这座城市参赛，实际上是这座城市培养体育人才和软实力的最好广告，”她说。孔解释说，运动员在国际舞台上的表现直接提升香港的国际形象，增强居民的归属感和自豪感。
她为精英体育训练提出了四个目标，包括培养顶尖运动员以提升香港在世界体育界的地位，以及展示香港的人才培养实力。她补充说，精英运动员可以激励年轻人从事体育运动，推动大众参与并建立社会凝聚力和自豪感。

香港表示，以精英体育为支柱，香港可以推动社区体育、保持重大国际赛事的枢纽地位、提高专业水平、打造体育产业、改善运动员退役后的道路并创造可持续的人才循环。

在谈到资源分配时，她指出，精英体育资金传统上侧重于通过主要投资于最有可能获得主要国际奖牌的运动员和学科来实现回报最大化。她敦促当局全面推广这一方法，同时推进人才输送、体育科学研究、场馆基础设施、大湾区合作和全球体育影响力。

孔特别强调早期人才发掘和双轨教育途径，平衡严格的训练与学术研究，确保全职运动生涯仍然是年轻人才的可行且安全的选择。为了实现训练方案的现代化，她建议更深入地整合运动科学，包括生物力学分析、生理跟踪、量身定制的营养计划和心理咨询。
她还呼吁政府申办重大国际赛事，实行国内设施与海外训练营相结合的混合训练模式。她建议与大湾区城市探索建立训练基地，创造更多比赛和交流机会，并敦促政府争取国际体育机构在香港设立地区总部或办事处，培养本地担任委员和裁判的人才，让香港在比赛规则上有更多发言权。

Hong Kong
Lawmaker and former Olympic fencer Vivian Kong Man-wai has called for an optimised elite sports training system, saying athletes are Hong Kong's best advertisement for soft power. Ahead of a Legco debate, she outlined four goals including talent pipelines, sports science, GBA cooperation and interna

[![Image 1: Adam](https://clb.org.hk/en/static/img/editors/clb-adam-192.png)](https://clb.org.hk/en/desks/clb-desk)

By [Adam](https://clb.org.hk/en/desks/clb-desk), Editor in Chief

19 Oct 2026 at 17:35 HKT · 2 min read

An optimised elite sports training system would sharpen Hong Kong athletes' competitive edge and serve as the city's strongest soft-power showcase on the global stage, athlete-turned-lawmaker Vivian Kong Man-wai has said.

Her remarks came ahead of a Legislative Council debate on Wednesday on a motion to improve elite sports training and support systems, following Hong Kong's historic 54-medal haul at the 20th Asian Games. In an interview with Sing Tao Daily, the sister publication of The Standard, the former Olympic fencing gold medallist expressed strong backing for sustained advancements in athlete development and institutional support.

"Athletes competing for the city are, in fact, the best advertisement for its ability to nurture sports talent and for its soft power," she said. Kong explained that athletes' performances on the international stage directly raise Hong Kong's global profile and strengthen residents' sense of belonging and pride.

She laid out four goals for elite sports training, including producing top athletes to lift Hong Kong's standing in world sports and showcasing its talent-nurturing strength. Elite athletes, she added, can inspire young people to take up sports, drive mass participation and build social cohesion and pride.

With elite sports as the anchor, Kong said Hong Kong can promote community sports, remain a hub for major international events, raise professionalism and build sports as an industry, improving athletes' post-retirement pathways and creating a sustainable talent cycle.

Addressing resource allocation, she noted that elite sports funding has traditionally focused on maximising returns by investing primarily in competitors and disciplines with the highest probability of securing major international medals. She urged authorities to expand this approach comprehensively by advancing talent pipelines, sports science research, venue infrastructure, Greater Bay Area cooperation and global sporting influence in tandem.

Kong placed special emphasis on early talent scouting and dual-track educational pathways that balance rigorous training with academic study, ensuring full-time athletic careers remain a viable and secure choice for young talent. To modernise training regimens, she recommended deeper integration of sports science, including biomechanical analysis, physiological tracking, tailored nutritional planning and psychological counselling.

She also called on the government to pursue bids for major international competitions and implement a hybrid training model combining domestic facilities with overseas training camps. She recommended exploring training bases with Greater Bay Area cities to create more competition and exchange opportunities, and urged the government to court international sports bodies into opening regional headquarters or offices in Hong Kong to nurture local talent as committee members and referees, giving the city more say over competition rules, resources and major-event bids.

title: Southeast Asia oxygen tanks, purifier sales spike
summary: **KUALA LUMPUR** — Toxic haze from wildfires burning in Indonesia has spiked a demand for oxygen tanks and air purifiers across the region, manufacturers say, as they work the clock on equipment providing life-saving clean air. The months-l
content:
**KUALA LUMPUR** — Toxic haze from wildfires burning in Indonesia has spiked a demand for oxygen tanks and air purifiers across the region, manufacturers say, as they work the clock on equipment providing life-saving clean air.

The months-long haze has blanketed parts of Southeast Asia, forcing school closures and fueling a rise in respiratory complaints. Families are now rushing to buy devices to keep indoor air clean.

At AA Alive, a medical equipment company based just outside of Kuala Lumpur, employees were working at full capacity to deliver oxygen bottles, with officials saying sales were rocketing.

“We have seen a 35 percent increase in sales because of the haze,” Rafina Firdaus, a member of AA Alive’s sales team, told Agence France-Presse (AFP) during a visit.

“When I started in the industry, I was shocked to see so many patients who need oxygen tanks,” she said.

The company supplies patients with both oxygen tanks and oxygen concentrators.

An oxygen tank can run for about three hours of continuous use, while a concentrator can be used for about 24 hours.

Md Noor Bin Bujang, 69, spent more than a month in hospital and received his first oxygen concentrator on Thursday evening.

He told AFP that without the oxygen-providing equipment he would have “a shortness of breath, especially with the haze.”

Mubassar Khan, a 26-year-old AA Alive technician, said an oxygen concentrator’s filter is normally replaced after 1,000 hours of usage, but the haze’s pollutants have halved its lifespan.

AA Alive currently delivers around 40 rental units per day, and Firdaus said the company was able to meet the increased demands caused by the haze because they have “already experienced it every year.”

AFP journalists saw close to 60 oxygen concentrators and around 20 oxygen tanks that were due for a service or replacement at the company’s showroom and warehouse.

## **‘Sharp surge’**

Experts warn prolonged exposure to haze pollutants could cause inflammation that is harmful to the body, with one classifying the situation as a “multisystem public health threat.”

Juliana Jalaludin, a professor specializing in environmental health at Universiti Putra Malaysia, told AFP she was worried that future generations could “experience a higher burden of respiratory illnesses if they are repeatedly exposed to haze and air pollution, particularly during childhood.”

“The key is to reduce exposure now to protect children’s health and prevent long-term consequences for future generations,” Juliana said.

Air purifier retailers, meanwhile, said sales have jumped since air quality levels started to dip in August during haze conditions.

“Recently, we have seen a 600 percent increase in sale volume of air purifier sales... from Sep 28 to Oct 12, compared to the same period last year,” regional consumer electronics retailer Courts said in a statement.

“Customers are becoming more conscious of indoor air quality and are actively exploring solutions to maintain a healthier and more comfortable home environment,” a Courts spokesman told AFP.

Singapore-based retailer Gain City said it has also seen “a significant increase in air-purifier demand.”

“Demand began picking up in recent weeks, with a particularly sharp surge from October 9. Sales have since risen to nine times the level recorded at the start of the haze season in August,” the company said. AFP

title: SA pushes for more money to adapt at COP31
summary: Severe climate shocks, record-breaking temperatures and devastating weather events worldwide have marked 2026 as a standout year for extreme climate events globally. South Africa has not been spared. In January, historic floods swept throug
content:
Severe climate shocks, record-breaking temperatures and devastating weather events worldwide have marked 2026 as a standout year for extreme climate events globally.

South Africa has not been spared. In January, historic floods swept through Limpopo and Mpumalanga, killing at least 30 people, damaging thousands of homes and causing billions of rands in infrastructure damage. Four months later, the Western Cape was hit, causing 11 fatalities, displacing over 200,000 people, and battering the province’s agricultural sector.

An unfolding Super El Niño threatens a hotter, drier summer marked by drought, wildfires, water shortages, food insecurity and heat-related illness, placing the responsibility on the government to safeguard residents from a warming world.

That is why, as South Africa heads to the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in November, increased adaptation finance is among the country’s top priorities in the climate negotiations.

### Adaptation and resilience

Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment Minister David Maynier said that the fact that, at only 4%, Africa’s emissions paled in the face of global greenhouse gas emissions made adaptation and resilience one of the main priorities for South Africa, given the country’s severe experience with storms, floods and drought.

Speaking at a national stakeholder consultation on South Africa’s negotiating mandate for COP31 on Friday, 16 October, Maynier said that South Africa’s negotiators would push for a benchmark to triple adaptation finance by 2035, the operationalisation of the global goal on adaptation, and adequate loss and damage funding.

Carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions from burning fossil fuels and industrial processes. This includes emissions from transport, electricity generation, and heating, but not land-use change. (Source: Our World in Data)

While the country’s negotiation team will focus heavily on adaptation, South Africa still has a case to answer for regarding the reduction of emissions. Granted, the country’s global emissions sit at 1.1% to 1.14%. However, the nation is[Africa’s biggest emitter](https://ourworldindata.org/profile/co2/south-africa), accounting for roughly 33% to more than 40% of the continent’s total emissions.

Maesela Kekana, the DFFE’s deputy director-general responsible for climate change and air quality, and the person who would lead the charge during the negotiations, said that nations had clear directions on what needed to be done on mitigation; however, the same could not be said for adaptation.

Maesela Kekana, the DFFE’s deputy director-general responsible for climate change and air quality. (Photo: Dianah Chiyangwa)

“On adaptation, we don’t really know where we are. Hence this Belém to Addis vision becomes quite important because it deals with key indicators that will tell us exactly how far we are in building resilience.”

Established during COP30 in Belém, Brazil, in 2025, the Belém–Addis Vision on Adaptation is a negotiation process intended to help countries put global adaptation goals into practice and measure progress towards them.

### **Loss and Damage fund needs a boost**

South Africa is one of 119 countries that have submitted more than 170 funding proposals to the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD). Maynier said that after the floods in January devastated the Kruger National Park and surrounding areas, the country submitted a $20-million proposal to restore the flood-affected and associated conservation landscapes.

Floods sweep through Letaba, Kruger National Park, in January 2026. (Photo: SANParks)

While progress has been made with a dedicated FRLD, Kekana said that South Africa sought greater support for the fund, adding that “there’s quite a big gap between what is required to deal with these permanent losses and damages and what is on the table”.

The FRLD supports developing countries and communities affected by climate-related disasters; however, the fund faces a massive budget and liquidity shortfall.

Responding to questions from Daily Maverick about the likelihood of South Africa receiving funding, given the sheer volume of requests and the money available in the fund, Maynier said he hoped the proposal would succeed, adding that bilateral talks had already taken place to advocate for it.

Kenana said that South Africa’s negotiating team would call for more resources for the fund, but would also seek assistance from other financial institutions outside the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) financial mechanisms, such as the Clean Investment Fund.

David Maynier. (Photo: Gallo Images / Luba Lesolle)

Dipak Patel, deputy chairperson of the Presidential Climate Commission, said South Africa’s request would prove to be a test for the loss and damage fund.

“South Africa should treat this as a test case of what South Africa can actually present [to the summit] that would meet or pass muster with respect to what is required.

“I see the potential for loss and damage to be extended to climate-impacted events, whether that be severe flooding in Durban or severe warming in other parts of the country.

“But let us be aware that in a context where we might not be suffering the most damage, any global fund would have to prioritise on the basis of vulnerability and on the basis of their own socioeconomic position,” Patel said.

A drone view shows houses flooded after heavy rains in Durban, South Africa, February 20, 2025. (Photo: REUTERS/Rogan Ward)

### **Nations to take stock on climate action**

The second Global Stocktake (GST) will begin during this year’s summit. The process serves as an inventory of the planet, where countries and stakeholders assess where they are succeeding and where they are falling short in meeting the Paris Climate Agreement. The GST, which takes two years to complete, aims to inform the next round of climate action plans (nationally determined contributions, or NDCs).

The GST, which takes place every five years, could not come at a more significant time. In September, the United Nations Environment Programme released a report that found a 1.5°C overshoot is now widely unavoidable and would occur within years, bringing more frequent extreme weather events globally.

The Greenland ice sheet, facing intensifying global warming, is melting. (Photo by Sean Gallup/Getty Images)

The report, titled[Limiting Overshoot: Navigating Exceedance of 1.5°C and Pathways Towards Return](https://www.unep.org/en/news-and-stories/press-release/unep-world-set-cross-15degc-global-warming-can-still-limit-adapt-and), found that best-case projections peaked at 1.8°C and others exceeded 2°C, and it proposed an “overshoot, peak and decline” strategy to minimise the risks of extreme weather, ecosystem loss and irreversible tipping points.

The strategy, which includes immediate emissions cuts, transformational adaptation and governed carbon dioxide removal, would theoretically bring the world back below 1.5°C warming.

TEMPERATURE OVERSHOOT: EXCEED AND RETURN TO 1.5°C
Decades of insufficient action have locked us into three compounding challenges to limiting temperature overshoot, with an urgent need for action now. (Source: United Nations)

According to the UNFCCC, the stocktake can help policymakers and stakeholders strengthen their climate policies and commitments in their next round of NDCs, paving the way for accelerated action.

Referring to the stocktake, Maynier said it should assess progress beyond emissions reductions and focus on advancing climate finance, technology transfer, capacity building for developing countries and addressing loss and damage. **DM**

Published: 6:00am, 17 Oct 2026 Updated: 10:54am, 18 Oct 2026

A US congressional committee has released details of [investigations into dozens of researchers](https://www.scmp.com/news/china/diplomacy/article/3358117/china-initiative-20-us-crackdown-chinese-scholars-intensifies?module=inline&pgtype=article), many of them Chinese-American, revealing the scale of government scrutiny sweeping academia over alleged links to China.

The documents – running to hundreds of pages – were released alongside a separate report by the House Select Committee on China. Titled “How to Stop China’s Theft of Taxpayer-Funded Research”, the report pushes back against arguments by universities and academic groups that tighter research security rules threaten academic freedom.

According to the committee, the records derive from investigations by the National Science Foundation’s Office of Inspector General (NSF OIG), including details of previously unreported cases.

# Taiwan bulks up on protein-packed bentos as obesity rates rise

Chain stores look to tap into growing health consciousness that spans generations

Customers come to The Protein Box bento chain in Taipei just after noon to get lunch.(Photo by Nikkei)

RYOSUKE EGUCHI

October 17, 2026 17:40 JST

Listen

English (Original)

[](https://twitter.com/share?text=Taiwan+bulks+up+on+protein-packed+bentos+as+obesity+rates+rise&url=https%3A%2F%2Fasia.nikkei.com%2Fbusiness%2Ffood-beverage%2Ftaiwan-bulks-up-on-protein-packed-bentos-as-obesity-rates-rise&via=NikkeiAsia)[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fasia.nikkei.com%2Fbusiness%2Ffood-beverage%2Ftaiwan-bulks-up-on-protein-packed-bentos-as-obesity-rates-rise)[](https://api.whatsapp.com/send?text=Taiwan+bulks+up+on+protein-packed+bentos+as+obesity+rates+rise+https%3A%2F%2Fasia.nikkei.com%2Fbusiness%2Ffood-beverage%2Ftaiwan-bulks-up-on-protein-packed-bentos-as-obesity-rates-rise)[](https://t.me/share/url?text=Taiwan+bulks+up+on+protein-packed+bentos+as+obesity+rates+rise&url=https%3A%2F%2Fasia.nikkei.com%2Fbusiness%2Ffood-beverage%2Ftaiwan-bulks-up-on-protein-packed-bentos-as-obesity-rates-rise)[](mailto:?subject=Taiwan%20bulks%20up%20on%20protein-packed%20bentos%20as%20obesity%20rates%20rise&body=https%3A%2F%2Fasia.nikkei.com%2Fbusiness%2Ffood-beverage%2Ftaiwan-bulks-up-on-protein-packed-bentos-as-obesity-rates-rise)

TOKYO -- High-protein meals are becoming increasingly popular in Taiwan, with specialty stores popping up and convenience store operators expanding lineups of such products as interest in health and fitness grows across age groups.

The Protein Box, a bento chain in a part of Taipei where offices and restaurants mingle, draws crowds of office workers from nearby buildings around noon. Customers range from young women to middle-aged men.

The company is built around the idea of healthy, low-fat, high-protein meals. Customers can choose a main dish of chicken, pork, beef or fish, served with boiled vegetables, eggs and rice. Meals cost 130 New Taiwan dollars to NT$150 ($4 to $4.70), and many contain more than 30 grams of protein.

Advertisement

The chain was founded in 2019 by a fitness enthusiast who was frustrated at being unable to find good meals after workouts. It has grown rapidly, primarily in urban areas, and now has 119 locations.

The high-protein trend has spread to convenience stores. At a 7-Eleven in Taipei, seven varieties of ready-to-eat chicken breast products line a single shelf. Refrigerated bento meals and noodle dishes carrying the word "protein" in their product names are also common.

President Chain Store, which operates 7-Eleven in Taiwan, markets a line of health-oriented products, with high-protein offerings proving especially popular. Two such bento products have sold more than 10 million servings combined over the past year.

The company's member data analysis shows the products are popular not only among consumers under 29 but also among people aged 50 and older. "They have become a common need shared by both younger and middle-aged consumers," the company said.

Japan-based FamilyMart has offered foods promoted as health-oriented since 2019, emphasizing high protein, high dietary fiber and reduced sugar content. The lineup includes high-protein soy milk and rice sandwiches made with chicken and egg.

One factor behind the trend is Taiwan's rising obesity rate. The share of adults classified as overweight -- indicating a body mass index (BMI) of 24 or higher but below 27 -- or obese, indicating a BMI of 27 or higher, has continued to increase, reaching 51.3% of people aged 18 and above in a survey covering 2020-24.

As Taiwan's population ages rapidly, authorities are encouraging companies, local governments and residents to promote exercise and improve eating habits.

Health consciousness has also evolved following the coronavirus pandemic, including in the growing use of fitness centers. World Gym Taiwan, the island's largest chain, expanded from 106 facilities at the end of 2021 to 146 as of this month.

Fitness Factory, another chain that has 86 locations, had 394,000 members as of June, up 30,000 from the end of 2025.

"We've seen people of all ages, from young adults to middle-aged and elderly consumers, begin placing greater importance on exercise," said the company's CFO, who estimates the number of paid gym users in Taiwan at around 1.1 million and predicts it will exceed 1.5 million within two to three years.

According to a 2025 survey by Taiwan's Sports Ministry, 35.6% of respondents said they exercised at least three times a week for 30 minutes or more per session, up 0.3 percentage points from the previous survey and the fifth consecutive year of gradual gains.

title: Japan Wants to Sell Air Defense, Maritime Surveillance Systems to Philippine Forces - USNI News
zh_title: 日本希望向菲律宾军队出售防空和海上监视系统 - USNI新闻
summary: 日本陆上自卫队的03型中程地对空导弹。日本陆上自卫队照片菲律宾马尼拉——日本希望向菲律宾出售防空、海上监视和反无人机系统，以加强其在南海和吕宋海峡的军事力量。周三，在日本自卫队成立 72 周年纪念日期间，拟议的中短程防空系统销售计划得到了强调。该提案代表了东京对马尼拉长期安全援助的新阶段，并且是在两国加强防务关系之后进行的。
content:
日本陆上自卫队的03型中程地对空导弹。日本陆上自卫队照片

菲律宾马尼拉——日本希望向菲律宾出售防空、海上监视和反无人机系统，以加强其在南海和吕宋海峡的军事力量。

周三，在日本自卫队成立 72 周年纪念日期间，拟议的中短程防空系统销售计划得到了强调。该提案代表了东京对马尼拉长期安全援助的新阶段，也是两国通过最近的联合训练和后勤协议加强防务关系之后的结果。

在成立周年纪念活动中，日本三菱电机公司和东芝公司展示了他们的防空系统。其中包括03型中程地对空导弹、11型近程防空系统和91型单兵便携式防空系统。日本自卫队正在积极使用所有这些系统。
菲律宾武装部队正在寻求为其下一个现代化计划采购数十套地对空导弹系统，以满足菲律宾空军、陆军和海军陆战队的防空需求。日本国防工业代表告诉 USNI 新闻，[最近修订的国防出口指南](https://www.trade.gov/market-intelligence/japan-defense-export-policy) 使得向菲律宾出售和转让这些日本制造的防空系统成为可能。

日本军事分析家稻叶义博告诉美国海军学院新闻网：“这些系统共同可以保护城市地区、关键基础设施和军事设施。通过整合这些系统，日本可以建立一个分层的防空网络，能够在多个层面上反击中国的空中攻击。”

2026 年 10 月 14 日，在日本自卫队成立 72 周年纪念活动期间，日本三菱电机公司和东芝公司展示了他们的防空系统。菲律宾国防部照片

稻叶表示，虽然东京正在扩大其国内导弹生产能力，但目前的扩张努力旨在加强日本自卫队的远程打击计划，可能不足以满足出口需求。
“扩大的导弹产能可能仍不足以满足出口需求。尽管如此，即使在向日本自卫队的导弹交付完成后，出口对于维持扩大的生产基地也至关重要，”稻叶说。

马尼拉尚未建立能够保护其广阔领空或拦截弹道导弹威胁的防空网络。菲律宾的主要对手中国部署了大量巡航导弹、弹道导弹和高超音速导弹，可以从各种地面、海军和空中平台向菲律宾基地发射。

除了防空提案外，日本公司还展示了天基和沿海雷达海上监视系统。其中一次演示中，日本卫星星座正在监测黄岩岛，这是一个[有争议的南海海洋地物](https://news.usni.org/2026/09/11/combat-patrol-scarborough-shoal)，也是菲律宾和中国之间各种对峙和冲突的发生地。展示了从固定站点到移动雷达的各种海上监视雷达，其中包括一种可以跟踪最远 75 海里目标的系统。

自 2010 年代以来，日本已资助 17

【原文 English Original】
Japan Ground Self-Defense Force’s Type 03 medium-range surface-to-air missile. JGSDF photo

MANILA, Philippines — Japan wants to sell air defense, maritime surveillance and counter-drone systems to the Philippines amid its push to bolster forces in the South China Sea and Luzon Strait.

The proposed sale of medium and short-range air defense systems was highlighted Wednesday on the sidelines of the 72nd founding anniversary of the Japan Self-Defense Force. The proposal represents a new phase in Tokyo’s longstanding security assistance to Manila and follows enhanced defense ties between the two countries through recent joint training and logistics agreements.

During the founding anniversary event, Japanese firms Mitsubishi Electric Corporation and Toshiba showcased their air defense systems. These included the Type 03 medium-range surface-to-air missile, Type 11 short-range air defense system and Type 91 man portable air defense system. All of these systems are in active use by the JSDF.

The Armed Forces of the Philippines is looking to procure dozens of batteries of surface-to-air missile systems for Philippine Air Force, Army and Marine Corps air defense requirements under its next modernization program. [Recently revised defense export guidelines](https://www.trade.gov/market-intelligence/japan-defense-export-policy) have made the sale and transfer of these Japanese-made air defense systems to the Philippines possible, a Japanese defense industry representative told USNI News.

“Together, these systems can protect urban areas, critical infrastructure and military installations. By integrating these systems, Japan can establish a layered air defense network capable of countering Chinese aerial attacks at multiple levels,” Yoshihiro Inaba, a Japanese military analyst, told USNI News.

Japanese firms Mitsubishi Electric Corporation and Toshiba showcased their air defense systems Oct. 14, 2026, on the sidelines of the 72nd founding anniversary of the Japan Self-Defense Force. Philippines Department of National Defense photo

While Tokyo is expanding its domestic missile production capabilities, the current expansion effort is aimed at strengthening the JSDF’s long-range strike plans and may prove inadequate for export demands, Inaba said.

“The expanded missile production capacity may still be insufficient to meet export demand. Nevertheless, exports will be essential to maintaining the expanded production base even after deliveries of missiles to the JSDF have been completed,” said Inaba.

Manila has yet to operate an air defense network capable of protecting its vast air space or intercepting ballistic missile threats. China, the Philippines primary adversary, fields a vast array of cruise, ballistic and hypersonic missiles that can be launched against Philippine bases from a variety of ground, naval and air platforms.

Alongside the air defense proposals, Japanese firms presented space-based and coastal radar maritime surveillance systems. One of these presentations saw a Japanese satellite constellation monitoring Scarborough Shoal, a [contested South China Sea maritime feature](https://news.usni.org/2026/09/11/combat-patrol-scarborough-shoal) that is the site of various standoffs and clashes between the Philippines and China. Various maritime surveillance radars ranging from fixed sites to mobile radars were showcased, including one system that could track targets up to 75 nautical miles away.

Since the 2010s, Japan has funded 17 Coast Guard cutters and sold four air surveillance radars to the Philippine Air Force. In 2023, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs launched the [Official Security Assistance program.](https://news.usni.org/2023/11/09/japan-grants-security-assistance-to-the-philippines-looks-to-enhance-military-cooperation) Under this program, the Philippines has received maritime patrol infrastructure, radar maintenance support and coastal surveillance systems. The Philippines and Japan are also [engaged in talks](https://news.usni.org/2026/06/03/philippines-progresses-japanese-destroyer-transfer-talks-receives-american-cutter-at-shangri-la) regarding the transfer of five Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force Abukuma-class destroyers. The transfer is set to occur within the next two to three years.

Beyond the potential for air defense transfers, Inaba said he expects future security assistance to the Philippines to include unmanned systems and transport vessels.

Last month, Japan launched the first of a series of British-designed high speed landing craft. Tokyo wants to use these vessels for the rapid insertion of troops and supplies across its Ryukus island chain, which covers a strategic strait near Taiwan.

“Such landing craft would be essential for transporting troops and supplies in support of the defense of the South China Sea,” said Inaba.

title: Underground railway set to reshape old Tainan, revive historic station - Focus Taiwan
zh_title: 地下铁路将重塑旧台南，复兴历史车站 - 聚焦台湾
summary: 中新社台南10月15日电 台南台南地下列车将于周六开始运行，标志着台南城市景观重塑迈出了重要一步，也为台南百年火车站作为了解当地历史文化的门户开辟了新的可能性。几代人以来，这条铁路一直是贯穿台湾最古老城市台南的重要南北交通走廊。但其轨道、平交路口、地下通道和立交桥也将城市分割开来，使得东部和西部地区之间的交通更加困难。据工信部称
content:
中新社台南10月15日电 台南台南地下列车将于周六开始运行，标志着台南城市景观重塑迈出了重要一步，也为台南百年火车站作为了解当地历史文化的门户开辟了新的可能性。

几代人以来，这条铁路一直是贯穿台湾最古老城市台南的重要南北交通走廊。但其轨道、平交路口、地下通道和立交桥也将城市分割开来，使得东部和西部地区之间的交通更加困难。

据交通部称，全长8.23公里的地下路段将取消23个铁路道口及相关建筑物，改善行人和骑自行车者的通行，同时缓解交通瓶颈。

该项目于2009年9月获得内阁批准，由铁路局牵头，历时约17年才实现第一阶段通车。据该局称，在此期间，成本从预计的 330 亿新台币增加到 412.6 亿新台币（13 亿美元），整个项目目前计划于 2031 年 3 月完工。

转型将不仅仅限于交通运输。交通部表示，一旦现有轨道被拆除，计划将原来的铁路走廊变成一条约30米宽的绿道，并设有步行道、自行车道和景观区，连接新车站、社区、学校和公共设施。
## 历史车站的新角色

国立成功大学建筑学荣休教授、车站修复和再利用计划审查委员会成员傅朝卿表示，该项目还提供了一个重新思考台南车站角色的机会，台南车站是该市最知名的地标之一。

该车站的历史建筑于 1936 年重建，并于 1998 年被指定为国家纪念碑。该车站于 1900 年日本殖民统治期间（1895-1945 年）首次开放。它将保留在新地铁站旁边，而不是被新地铁站取代。

傅说，车站与台南的城市布局紧密相关。它面向车站环岛和历史悠久的市中心的位置决定了人们进入和游览城市的方式。

铁路规划者最初考虑在更北的地方建造一个新车站，将历史建筑抛在后面，傅反对这一提议，因为这可能会切断车站与市中心的长期关系。

采用的设计将新车站置于地下并毗邻历史建筑，使两者共存。其低矮的水平轮廓和宽阔的天篷使旧车站在视觉上更加突出，而下沉的广场和连接的走道将两个设施连接起来。
台铁表示，旧车站还可以发挥更重要的文化和商业作用，并补充说，正在讨论的计划包括咖啡馆、便餐选择、当地纪念品、阅读空间和展览。

## 连接交通和遗产

成大城市规划系特聘教授陈彦仲表示，铁路迁入地下也为保留和诠释车站周围的历史风貌提供了机会。

台南已有400多年的历史，曾是台湾的省会，保留了历史悠久的铁路设施和车站周围的其他历史遗迹，包括站台、转盘、仓库和车站等。

【原文 English Original】
Tainan, Oct. 15 (CNA) Trains are set to begin running underground in Tainan on Saturday, marking a major step in reshaping the southern Taiwan city's urban landscape and opening up new possibilities for its century-old railway station to serve as a gateway to local history and culture.

For generations, the railway has served as a vital north-south transportation corridor through Tainan, Taiwan's oldest city. But its tracks, level crossings, underpasses and overpasses have also divided the city, making travel between its eastern and western districts more difficult.

According to the Ministry of Transportation and Communications (MOTC), the 8.23-kilometer underground section will eliminate 23 railway crossings and related structures, improving access for pedestrians and cyclists while easing traffic bottlenecks.

Approved by the Cabinet in September 2009 and led by the Railway Bureau, the project will have taken about 17 years to reach its first-stage opening. In that period the cost rose from a projected NT$33 billion to NT$41.26 billion (US$1.3 billion), with the full project now scheduled for completion in March 2031, according to the bureau.

The transformation will extend beyond transportation. Once the existing tracks are removed, there are plans to turn the former railway corridor into a greenway about 30 meters wide, with walking and cycling paths and landscaped areas linking new stations, neighborhoods, schools and public facilities, the MOTC said.

## A new role for a historic station

The project also offers an opportunity to rethink the role of Tainan Station, one of the city's most recognizable landmarks, said Fu Chao-ching (傅朝卿), an emeritus professor of architecture at National Cheng Kung University (NCKU) and a member of the review committee for the station's restoration and reuse plan.

First opened in 1900 during Japanese colonial rule (1895-1945), the station's historic building was rebuilt in 1936 and designated a national monument in 1998. It will remain in place alongside the new underground station rather than be replaced by it.

Fu said the station is closely tied to Tainan's urban layout. Its position facing the station roundabout and the historic city center has shaped how people enter and navigate the city.

Railway planners initially considered building a new station further north, leaving the historic building behind, a proposal Fu opposed because it risked severing the station's long-standing relationship with the city center.

The adopted design instead places the new station underground and next to the historic building, allowing the two to coexist. Its low, horizontal profile and broad canopy give visual prominence to the old station, while a sunken plaza and connecting walkways link the two facilities.

The old station could also take on a more prominent cultural and commercial role, Taiwan Railway Corp. said, adding that plans under discussion include cafes, light meals options, local souvenirs, reading spaces and exhibitions.

## Connecting transport and heritage

The railway's relocation underground also presents an opportunity to preserve and interpret the historic features around the station, said Chen Yen-chung (陳彥仲), a distinguished professor in NCKU's Department of Urban Planning.

With a history of more than 400 years, Tainan was once the capital of Taiwan and retains historic railway facilities and other remnants of the past around the station, including platforms, a turntable, warehouses and sections of the old city wall.

Chen said future development should balance preservation with new uses, allowing the station to serve as a starting point for understanding Tainan's history and culture.

He said rather than simply passing through the station to transfer to other forms of transportation, visitors could encounter the city's past there before continuing to historic areas such as the old city center and Anping.

"Restrictions should not be seen as limitations. They can instead become opportunities to create a distinctive urban character," Chen said.

The project has also revealed traces of Tainan's earlier history beneath the modern city. According to the city's Cultural Affairs Bureau, construction teams uncovered 20 archaeological sites containing remains dating from prehistoric times to the Qing dynasty and Japanese colonial period.

The discoveries directly impacted the project's construction schedule, with archaeological investigations and preservation work adding about two years to the original timetable, the Railway Bureau said.

According to the Tainan City government, there were also design changes to preserve archaeological remains, either by relocating them for safekeeping or reinforcing them in place.

However, the transformation will take time. After trains begin running underground, the existing tracks and structures still need to be removed, roads restored and pedestrian facilities improved before the full benefits can be realized.

Two additional underground commuter stations, Linsen and South Tainan, are scheduled to open in 2029 and 2030, respectively.

The longer-term challenge will be to ensure that the land freed up by the project becomes useful public space, encourages renewal along the corridor and helps reconnect communities, Chen said.

For Tainan, the railway's move underground could ultimately reshape more than the city's transport network. Whether the former railway corridor becomes a meaningful public space, and whether the historic station can draw visitors into the city's wider cultural landscape, will help determine how far the project succeeds in reconnecting Tainan with its past as well as its future.

(By Chiu Chu-yin, Chang Jung-hsiang, Huang Chiao-wen and Lee Hsin-Yin)

title: “Secure and controllable”: How Beijing is writing Europe out of its systems
summary: In June 2025, a Chinese state-owned utility put out a tender covering the replacement of the control systems for 67 wind turbines at the Kangbao wind farm in Hebei. The turbines were not broken or outdated. The problem was their controllers
content:
In June 2025, a Chinese state-owned utility put out a tender covering the replacement of the control systems for 67 wind turbines at the Kangbao wind farm in Hebei. The turbines were not broken or outdated. The problem was their controllers, which were imported from Europe. The tender warned not only of high costs and long procurement cycles, but also of a risk of being “controlled by foreign forces”. The prescribed solution was replacement with domestically produced technology.

The Kangbao case is not unusual. A [new study](https://www.osw.waw.pl/designed-out/) by the Centre for Eastern Studies (OSW) of the Chinese wind sector analysed more than 1,600 publicly available procurement documents and found nearly 300 calling for foreign equipment to be replaced. European manufacturers and component suppliers are among those named in the notices as risks to be removed.

The analysis shows that Beijing’s drive to make its energy infrastructure “self-reliant, safe and controllable” is security-focused and discriminates against foreign suppliers, including European ones. And while European suppliers are written out of Chinese critical energy infrastructure, Chinese companies push for expansion in Europe.

It is widely known that China’s leadership under Xi Jinping strives for China to be less reliant on technology imports, especially in critical infrastructure. OSW’s findings describe how this is being done and how European firms are affected. They show a coordinated effort, more than a decade in the making, to identify foreign technological dependencies that could become vulnerabilities, build domestic alternatives and gradually remove the foreign technology itself.

The findings should reassure Europeans already moving towards a more restrictive approach. Reciprocity used to mean asking Beijing to open its market, follow rules and stop discriminating. This notion no longer fits the reality. Europeans need to re-evaluate their understanding of security in critical infrastructure, and to shift what they mean by “reciprocity”: not waiting for China to match Europe’s openness, but matching China’s protective measures.

## China’s path to technological self-reliance and control

The OSW research shows that as early as 2012 Chinese State Council documents warned that core information technologies depended on other countries. The 2015 National Security Law made the development of “self-reliant and controllable” critical technologies a national-security objective. In 2016, Xi Jinping described having core technologies controlled by others as China’s “greatest hidden danger”.

What followed was a three-stage process: creating alternatives, ensuring demand and replacing vulnerabilities. The 14th Five-Year Plan called for manufacturing to become “self-reliant and controllable, safe and efficient”. The 15th Five-Year Plan extended this into industrial-control software, precision bearings, motors, control systems and energy equipment—all areas where European companies retain important capabilities.

At the same time, Beijing has understood that diversification away from non-Chinese inputs could not just be ordered. Someone had to buy the alternatives to ensure the investments were worthwhile. Regulation securing that demand followed: operators were required to prioritise “secure and trustworthy” products; acceptable technologies for electricity systems were set out in official whitelists; and state-owned enterprises were obliged to support indigenous technological innovation.

The last stage is across-the-board substitution, and the OSW study shows the concrete manifestation of this in the energy sector. Since 2022, major state-owned energy utilities have translated the policy approach into their own procurement requirements. Their objections to imported systems are partly practical—poor reliability, slow spare-part delivery—and partly political: not “secure and controllable” and vulnerable to control by “foreign forces”.

In the wind sector, the campaign focuses on systems used to operate and control power assets. The technologies being targeted point to perceived risks of remote disruption and loss of control over power generation stemming from foreign presence in software, databases and other connected elements of critical infrastructure.

## Use China’s risk map to identify Europe’s vulnerabilities

The EU should treat China’s localisation agenda as a guide to how Beijing assesses strategic risk. China does not seek to localise every technology at once. Instead, it sets short- and long-term localisation objectives, and concentrates resources on selected capabilities and parts of the technological stack. Those choices therefore offer a window into which dependencies Beijing considers most dangerous. It is a playbook from which the EU can take inspiration as it weighs its [own trade-offs](https://ecfr.eu/publication/trust-and-trade-offs-how-to-manage-europes-green-technology-dependence-on-china/?amp)—which dependencies are worth the cost of removing and which are not.

The useful lesson is in the prioritisation: where Beijing is prepared to accept foreign dependence, where it seeks to reduce it and where it is willing to spend heavily to eliminate it. The Chinese leadership’s focus on the threat of remote disruption and loss of control to foreign actors over power generation points, in reverse, at the strategic vulnerability that Chinese technologies with remote access create in Europe.

When Beijing judges a technology sensitive enough to demand domestic control, European authorities should ask themselves what vulnerability it is seeking to close and whether Europe faces an equivalent exposure through Chinese suppliers. Europe should pay as much attention to what Chinese companies are eliminating from their own critical systems as to what Beijing wants to sell abroad.

## Decide on high-risk suppliers at EU level

Designating high-risk suppliers and third countries, and imposing mitigation measures, should sit at the EU level. Information and communications technology (ICT) risks cross national borders. In energy, disruption to grid infrastructure or generation assets can have cascading effects beyond the country where it originates, as the [2025 Iberian blackout](https://ecfr.eu/article/a-brighter-future-why-upgrading-the-grid-is-vital-for-europes-competitiveness/?amp) demonstrated. EU-level mitigation measures close the loophole that fragmented implementation creates: a supplier judged to pose an unacceptable security risk in one member state must not be able to simply shift its business to another.

EU-level designations also take the political pressure off individual member states. The [5G Toolbox](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/eu-toolbox-5g-security), the European Commission’s non-binding framework for mitigating cyber-security risks in telecommunications infrastructure, is the lesson in what happens otherwise. Five years after its adoption, only [13 of the EU’s 27 member states](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:52026SC0156) had imposed restrictions on high-risk suppliers, though 22 had the legal powers to do so. Parts of Europe’s 5G infrastructure remain dependent on high-risk vendors, with Germany the most prominent example. Eight years after the debate about these vulnerabilities started, about [60%](https://www.lightreading.com/6g/huawei-5g-deal-defended-by-deutsche-telekom-boss-as-6g-ban-looms) of its radio access network is still provided by Chinese vendors. The share of European vendors present in China’s critical advanced communication systems has since fallen to [less than 3%](https://www.techtimes.com/articles/324592/20260815/nokia-closes-china-rd-hub-5g-world-splits-rival-supply-chains.htm).

## Radically rethink reciprocity

> **“**Beijing criticises the revised Cybersecurity Act as unfairly targeting Chinese companies, while its own procurement notices explicitly name European companies as supply-chain risks to be removed from critical infrastructure.”

Beijing’s [complaints](https://ec.europa.eu/info/law/better-regulation/have-your-say/initiatives/14578-The-EU-Cybersecurity-Act/F33393498_en) about Europe’s risk mitigation actions should be met with a plain and pragmatic observation: China does the same, more extensively and less transparently. Beijing [criticises](https://www.chinadaily.com.cn/a/202604/20/WS69e619c4a310d6866eb44785.html) the revised Cybersecurity Act as unfairly targeting Chinese companies, while its own procurement notices explicitly name European companies as supply-chain risks to be removed from critical infrastructure. Its grounds go well beyond technical faults or security incidents: a supplier’s foreign origin is itself disqualifying under a top-down localisation drive.

Under the revised Cybersecurity Act, whether a third country itself excludes EU-origin products from critical infrastructure should be considered when the EU assesses non-technical cyber risks. The EU should stress its own “[legitimate right](https://english.mofcom.gov.cn/News/SpokesmansRemarks/art/2026/art_6ba67ba24946452099098f1c83e3f408.html)”, in Beijing’s own phrase, to protect critical infrastructure, and use the evidence of China’s localisation drive to address asymmetric procurement conditions through the [International Procurement Instrument](https://ecfr.eu/publication/brussels-holdem-european-cards-against-trumpian-coercion/?amp). Trust cannot be a one-way street. Chinese companies should not compete freely for EU public contracts while European firms face systematic exclusion or replacement in China.

Europe is facing a less integrated world: supply chains are already concentrated in a few places, while global technology and energy systems are fragmenting. Openness itself is no longer a virtue, but increasingly a vulnerability. Those trends are not going to reverse any time soon. By eliminating European exposure in its own energy infrastructure, the Chinese leadership has set the tone. It is on Europe to take the message.
